transcript:
Header:
Date/Time: 2025-04-09 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~28 minutes
Location: Zoom
Recording: enabled
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Kapoor (Redwood SE), Diego Martin (Redwood SE), Jordan Lee (Quantix Head of ML), Maya Patel (Quantix SRE), Samir Gupta (Quantix Platform), Tess O'Neill (Quantix ML Eng)

Summary:
Deep technical session focused on throughput tuning for Redwood runtime: continuous batching behavior, scheduler knobs (slo vs throughput tradeoffs), max_num_seqs and per-worker token limits, KV cache effects on tail-latency, and quantization impacts on throughput. Discussed tradeoffs for Quantix's production workload (variable seq lengths, latency SLO 200ms p99 for short requests, bulk scoring for long sequences). Agreed next steps: Redwood to run a benchmark with Quantix sample traffic, share config checklist, and plan pilot kickoff.

Topics:
- Continuous batching and batching windows
- Scheduler knobs: max_batch_delay_ms, max_num_seqs, fairness vs throughput
- Token limits, per-worker concurrency, and KV cache warmup/eviction
- Quantization (int8 vs int4) throughput gains and rare quality regressions
- VPC / on-prem network considerations for control plane + cache locality

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, um, we'll dive right in. Quick roll call, Redwood on my side Alex and Priya and Diego, Quantix, Jordan?
[00:08] Jordan Lee: Yep that's me, Maya and Samir and Tess on the line. Morning folks.
[00:13] Priya Kapoor: Cool, so goal for today is to go deep on throughput tuning, like continuous batching and scheduler knobs, and figure out what settings make sense for your mixed workload.
[00:21] Samir Gupta: Sounds good, our main user path is lots of short chatty requests ~ 30-128 tokens, and then periodic bulk scoring jobs with 2k+ tokens. We care about short tail-latency p99 under 200ms and cost for bulk under an hour.
[00:36] Alex Chen: Great, that combination is exactly where continuous batching helps, but you can't just max it out. We'll walk through knobs.
[00:42] Priya Kapoor: Quick note — some transcriptions call it K V cash or K V cache, but I'll say KV cache for key-value attention cache, and it matters for long sequences because warm cache avoids re-compute.
[00:53] Tess O'Neill: When you say warm cache, do you mean per-model shard or per-worker? We're running sharded models across 4 GPUs.
[01:02] Priya Kapoor: Good question. The cache is per worker process; with sharded model shards each worker keeps its own slice of the KV cache for active requests. So cache locality depends on your routing and sticky sessions.
[01:13] Jordan Lee: Uh-huh ok. So what's the recommended max_num_seqs setting if we have mixed short and long requests?
[01:20] Priya Kapoor: Typically we set max_num_seqs to the median concurrent sequences per worker under typical load. For your mix, start with max_num_seqs=8 for the short-request tier and 2 for long-runner workers, then use smart routing to send bulk jobs to dedicated workers. The idea is, if you put too high a max_num_seqs you spin up long sequences in the same batch and they blow out latency.
[01:37] Maya Patel: That routing — is that automatic in Redwood or we must configure two pools?
[01:41] Diego Martin: Both. You can configure smart routing policies to prefer low-latency pool for short requests and batch pool for long jobs, or create two dedicated nodepools: low-latency and bulk. For on-prem we recommend separate worker labels and a routing rule.
[01:55] Samir Gupta: Does continuous batching introduce head-of-line blocking? We worry that batching waits for more short requests and delays immediate responses.
[02:01] Priya Kapoor: Continuous batching uses a micro-batching window. Two knobs: max_batch_delay_ms and target_batch_size. If you set max_batch_delay_ms=8-12ms and a target_batch_size low like 4-8, you reduce HOL blocking. For high throughput, larger windows and bigger target batch sizes increase throughput but increase single-request latency.
[02:18] Jordan Lee: Any rule of thumb for target_batch_size for 8xA100 or similar?
[02:22] Priya Kapoor: It really depends on model and token length distribution. For an 8xA100 serving a 7B-ish model, target_batch_size 16-32 often hits a good throughput point for medium sequences. But again, use a per-route config; short-chat route could be 4, scoring route 64.
[02:36] Tess O'Neill: Ok. Can you explain scheduler fairness — we saw docs mentioning fairness vs throughput tradeoffs.
[02:43] Diego Martin: Sure. The scheduler can prioritize latency-sensitive requests with weightening. If fairness is strict, throughput drops because scheduler spends cycles avoiding starving long jobs. If you skew to throughput, latency-sensitive requests might see higher p99. We expose a scheduling_alpha or fairness_ratio knob — lower alpha -> more throughput, higher alpha -> more fairness.
[03:02] Maya Patel: Is that the same as the preemption policy? Like can a low-latency request preempt an in-flight batch?
[03:08] Priya Kapoor: Not preemption in the CPU sense, but the scheduler will attempt to pack batches so latency-sensitive items get earlier batch slots. Preemption is expensive for GPU-run sequences since you lose in-flight compute. We recommend isolation via separate pools rather than aggressive preemption.
[03:25] Jordan Lee: Let's talk KV cache warmup — when a long sequence arrives, first tokens are slower while cache builds up, right?
[03:32] Priya Kapoor: Correct. There's a cache-warmup penalty for the first few KV steps per sequence. For long-running sessions we keep KV cached, but for ephemeral single-shot long requests you'll pay that cost. We mitigate with a warmup policy: if many requests share prefixes, prefix caching avoids re-warm. Also recommend sticky routing so follow-up tokens hit same worker.
[03:51] Samir Gupta: For bulk scoring, should we disable KV cache to save memory and increase throughput?
[03:56] Priya Kapoor: You can disable KV for stateless scoring when sequence length is small per item, but for very long sequences KV saves compute. For scoring many short candidates, KV doesn't help and disabling can reduce memory footprint.
[04:08] Alex Chen: Also note that quantization affects KV size — int8/int4 reduce memory and let you fit larger max_num_seqs per worker, increasing throughput. But watch for small accuracy regressions in int4 on some LLM ops.
[04:22] Tess O'Neill: Has Redwood seen big throughput wins from int8 or int4? What's safe?
[04:27] Priya Kapoor: Yes, int8 usually gives 1.6-2x throughput improvements and int4 can go further 2.5-3x depending on kernel support. But we run a quick eval suite to compare generation quality on critical prompts before pushing int4 to production. For safety, start int8 on prod, trial int4 on a canary.
[04:44] Jordan Lee: For on-prem, does quantization change any deployment requirements?
[04:48] Diego Martin: Not materially. You need kernel support in the runtime and matching compilers for your GPU. Some older drivers might not have optimal int4 kernels. Our on-prem installer checks for compatible CUDA/cuDNN and will warn if certain kernels are suboptimal.
[05:02] Maya Patel: Network: if the control plane is SaaS and data plane on-prem, do we see latency hit on KV cache or batching?
[05:09] Priya Kapoor: The control plane talk is infrequent — config, metrics, heartbeats. The hot path is local inference on the data plane. For VPC peering you need to ensure low latency between your workers and any optional managed cache or routing service. If you're using Redwood-managed caching over network, that's a no-go for latency-sensitive flows — we recommend local KV on worker for p99-sensitive workloads.
[05:29] Samir Gupta: Ok that matches our concern — we'll aim for private control plane but local data plane.
[05:35] Alex Chen: Back to knobs — token limits per-worker: set a max_tokens_in_flight or max_total_tokens param. This prevents a few huge requests from consuming GPU memory and evicting other workloads. Set it to slightly above your expected working set; e.g. if bulk jobs avg 2k tokens and you want 4 concurrent, set max_total_tokens ~ 8k.
[05:56] Tess O'Neill: And if a request would exceed the limit, do you reject or queue?
[06:00] Priya Kapoor: The runtime can either reject with 503 or queue depending on your policy. For low-latency routes we reject quickly; for batch routes we prefer queueing with backpressure. You can set a per-route behavior.
[06:12] Jordan Lee: We saw occasional tail latency spikes; are those usually scheduling or GC/serializing events?
[06:18] Diego Martin: Often scheduling and cache eviction. Also model compilation or kernel JIT at first inference can spike; we recommend warmup runs after deployment. GC in the service is minimal; most spikes are memory pressure evictions or hotspot batches mixing long/short sequences.
[06:33] Maya Patel: Do you have recommended warmup scripts?
[06:36] Priya Kapoor: Yes we'll share a small warmup script — it runs representative sequences across your routes at low QPS for 5-10 minutes to populate caches and JIT kernels. Action item.
[06:46] Alex Chen: Let's talk measurement — when you run benchmarks, please provide distribution histograms for sequence length and per-token think time, and specify concurrency. Priya will use that to recommend target_batch_size and max_num_seqs.
[06:59] Priya Kapoor: For benchmarks, we'll run two patterns: steady-state short-request stream at target QPS for 30 mins, and bulk scoring jobs queued to saturate GPUs for 1 hour. We'll capture p50/p95/p99 and token/sec.
[07:12] Jordan Lee: What's an expected token/sec improvement when enabling continuous batching vs naive single-request scheduling?
[07:18] Priya Kapoor: For typical small-medium models, continuous batching can improve token/sec by 2x-4x depending on batch packing efficiency and model size. The key is packing sequences of similar lengths to avoid padding waste.
[07:31] Samir Gupta: About padding waste — do you support dynamic batching where sequences padded to max in batch, or some packing strategy?
[07:37] Diego Martin: We do packing to minimize padding — sequences are grouped by length buckets, and the scheduler tries to fill batches with similar-len requests. You can configure bucket depth. That reduces wasted compute vs naive padding to max.
[07:50] Tess O'Neill: On the topic of bucket depth, how fine-grained should buckets be?
[07:54] Priya Kapoor: For mixed workloads, buckets of 16-32 token ranges work well. Too many buckets and scheduling overhead rises; too few and padding waste increases.
[08:03] Jordan Lee: Any caveats for chat sessions where context grows? We have users with progressive context growth over many turns.
[08:09] Priya Kapoor: For chat, KV cache shines: you keep the KV for the session so subsequent turns are fast. But remember you need sticky sessions or a centralized session router so the same worker gets follow-ups. Also plan for cache eviction policies for long-running chats — set TTL or max_kv_entries per session.
[08:25] Maya Patel: If a worker gets a very long chat and evicts other sessions' KV, is there an automatic spillover?
[08:31] Diego Martin: We don't spill KV across workers; eviction frees memory and increases re-warm cost for those evicted sessions. That's why capacity planning and route isolation is critical.
[08:41] Jordan Lee: Let's go through a concrete example — we have 200 qps of short chat (avg 60 tokens) and once an hour a bulk scoring window that submits 10k items at 1k tokens each over 15 minutes. How to configure?
[08:54] Priya Kapoor: I'd suggest two pools: pool-A low-latency with max_num_seqs 8, target_batch_size 6, max_batch_delay_ms 8, and strict rejection policy over queueing; pool-B bulk with larger max_num_seqs 32, target_batch_size 128, max_batch_delay_ms 50, and queueing enabled. Route short chat to pool-A, scoring to pool-B. For scoring, consider quantizing to int8 to fit more sequences per GPU.
[09:20] Tess O'Neill: For the bulk pool, does continuous batching wait to fill 128 before dispatching? The max_batch_delay_ms forces a timeout right?
[09:27] Priya Kapoor: Exactly. The scheduler dispatches when either target_batch_size is reached or max_batch_delay_ms passes. So you won't wait indefinitely.
[09:33] Samir Gupta: What about per-request priority? If a high-priority short request hits the bulk pool, can it jump?
[09:39] Diego Martin: We support priority tags and pre-batching priority — high-priority requests get placed in a fast lane and are scheduled earlier but again, for strict p99 we recommend isolation.
[09:48] Jordan Lee: On observability, will we see token-level heatmaps and per-route cost?
[09:53] Alex Chen: Yes Redwood Console gives token-level cost, per-route latency breakdown, and you can trace requests from API to worker to kernel. We'll show you a dashboard snapshot in the follow-up.
[10:03] Maya Patel: About kernel selection and JIT — do runtime compiles happen during production? We saw one of our early runs had a 2s spike that looked like a JIT.
[10:11] Priya Kapoor: Initial kernel GEMM selection or JIT can cause a spike. That's why warmup runs are important. After warmup the kernels are cached and subsequent calls are fast. On multi-tenant shared nodes this can occasionally repeat if kernels are evicted.
[10:24] Jordan Lee: Any metrics we should watch to detect padding inefficiencies?
[10:28] Diego Martin: Look at effective_token_utilization — ratio of useful tokens to total tokens processed. Low numbers indicate padding waste. Also per-batch padding histogram.
[10:36] Tess O'Neill: Are there built-in autotuners to find good target_batch_size/max_num_seqs?
[10:40] Priya Kapoor: We have an Optimize engine that suggests initial settings based on your workload profile and past benchmarks. It gives recommended configs you can apply as a starting point. It's not fully automatic in prod — we leave final decisions to operators.
[10:52] Jordan Lee: For the benchmark you're going to run, what do you need from us?
[10:56] Priya Kapoor: Sample request traces with timestamp, sequence length distribution, concurrency targets, and model/version. Also a small dataset for canary quality evals if we test int4.
[11:06] Samir Gupta: We'll scrub PII, send synthetic traces. Anything else?
[11:09] Priya Kapoor: Also your preferred latency SLOs per route and your maximum acceptable cost uplift for the pilot.
[11:16] Alex Chen: Quick note on failure modes — when a worker OOMs it's usually due to poorly constrained max_total_tokens or oversized batch packing. We instrument OOMs and recommend auto-scaling thresholds plus setting conservative token limits initially.
[11:31] Maya Patel: For on-prem VPC peering, anything special for security?
[11:35] Diego Martin: Ensure your firewall allows internal worker RPC ports and any managed sidecars. If you want private control plane, we offer an air-gapped control plane deploy — but that's a heavier setup. For VPC peering keep control plane endpoints inside your VPC or use our private endpoint option.
[11:50] Jordan Lee: Are audit logs detailed enough for compliance?
[11:53] Alex Chen: Yes we have request-level audit logs, encryption at rest and in flight, SSO/SAML integration. We'll include our SOC2 doc in follow-up.
[12:01] Tess O'Neill: One more question on batching — does Redwood support per-route override so we don't have to create separate pools for many tiny routes?
[12:08] Priya Kapoor: Yes per-route config overrides are supported. You can set target_batch_size, max_batch_delay_ms, and priority per route. Pools are useful when you want hardware isolation though.
[12:19] Jordan Lee: Cool. Let's recap next steps.
[12:22] Alex Chen: Recap: Redwood shares throughput tuning checklist and warmup scripts (Alex); Priya runs a benchmark on Quantix traffic and returns CSV results (Priya); Quantix sends sample traces and topology (Samir); schedule pilot kickoff week of 2025-04-21 (Alex to coordinate). We'll also send security and on-prem install checklist.
[12:41] Samir Gupta: Sounds good. Any other blockers?
[12:44] Jordan Lee: Not from my side. We'll get the traces over by 2025-04-14.
[12:49] Alex Chen: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up in email with links to docs and the calendar invite.
[12:54] Diego Martin: Thanks all.
[12:56] End of recording.
